identification.name: Polycarbonate (PC)
identification.common_form_notes: Widely stocked as extruded sheet and plate (e.g. Lexan/Makrolon) for machining, laser/CNC cutting, and cold/hot bending — the values here are for extruded sheet, not injection-molded parts, since sheet stock is the form students actually buy and machine. Injection-molded PC properties can differ somewhat with wall thickness and molding conditions. Also available as FDM filament, though it needs a high-temperature hotend/bed and an enclosure; FDM-printed parts will be weaker and anisotropic compared to the sheet-stock values here (see the ABS entry in this database for representative FDM anisotropy figures).
identification.notes: Values from MatWeb's aggregate "Overview of materials for Polycarbonate, Extruded" page, filtered to extruded grades specifically (unlike a similarly-named Nylon 12 aggregate found to be contaminated with reinforced grades, this one's ranges are all physically plausible for neat PC — no red flags). Grade counts behind the stored values: density n=102, tensile strength n=68, yield strength n=74, elongation n=82, Young's modulus n=66, CTE (coefficient of thermal expansion) n=63, thermal conductivity n=43, glass transition n=15, max/min service temperature n=9 each. PC is amorphous, not semi-crystalline — the melting point is left null even though the source reports a "Melting Point" figure (220–315 °C, avg 282 °C), since that almost certainly reflects a processing/softening range rather than a true first-order melting transition; the glass transition temperature (147 °C) is the physically meaningful thermal transition for this material and is well-attested (matches the commonly-cited textbook PC Tg of ~145–150 °C). Hardness reported on the Rockwell M scale (ASTM (American Society for Testing and Materials) D785, standard for rigid plastics), not Vickers/Brinell. Shear strength not directly reported — derived via von Mises: UTS (ultimate tensile strength)/√3 = 65.9/1.732 ≈ 38.1 MPa. Known for excellent impact toughness and low-temperature ductility (elongation at break ~89% average, minimum service temperature down to ≈ −47 °C) — notably tougher than acrylic, which is its main design tradeoff (PC is much less scratch/solvent resistant and more expensive than acrylic).

typical_usage: Impact-resistant machine guards and safety glazing, protective enclosures and windows, light covers/lenses, riot shields, and applications needing high impact toughness with reasonable optical clarity where acrylic would be too brittle. Choose PC over acrylic when impact resistance matters more than scratch resistance, weatherability, or cost.
